intro: Astronaut candidates combine training in the supersonic T-38 trainer, high-altitude aircraft, altitude chambers, and land/water survival to sharpen judgment and crew coordination in high-stress environments. Ellington Field at the Johnson Space Center serves as the hub for flight training.
lessons.0.title: Flight proficiency is the essence of spaceflight preparation
lessons.0.summary: The goal of T-38 training is not simply 'to become a pilot,' but to build the physical and habitual capacity to remain calm and make sound judgments under high-G, high-speed, and abnormal attitude conditions, while maintaining communication with the crew and ground control.
lessons.0.body.0: NASA has used the T-38 for astronaut flight proficiency training since the early 1960s. Flight operations at the Johnson Space Center are based at Ellington Field, where astronaut training is the primary mission. Regardless of prior pilot experience, candidates use the aircraft to cultivate confidence, teamwork, adaptability, and resilience in high-risk environments.
lessons.0.body.1: Official training descriptions explain that the T-38 simulates the G-forces, spatial disorientation, and the simultaneous processing of overlapping maneuvers and radio communications found during launch. The crew of Artemis II also refined their spatial awareness and adaptability to dynamic flight conditions using the T-38 at Ellington Field, in addition to classroom and simulator sessions.
lessons.0.body.2: During the summer training of the 2025 selection class, candidates flew the WB-57, a long-range high-altitude aircraft used for research flights since the 1960s, and began supersonic flight in the T-38. Candidates also perform maintenance tasks, such as using wrenches on the aircraft in the maintenance area. Since maintenance personnel cannot be called in orbit, the pilot's understanding of the aircraft is essential for spacecraft maintenance.

lessons.0.deepDive.title: Official Flight Time Guidelines
lessons.0.deepDive.body.0: NASA's Astronaut Selection and Training overview (2011) states that pilot astronauts maintain proficiency of 15 hours per month in the T-38, while non-pilots maintain a minimum of 4 hours per month. While these numbers may vary by era and operations, the policy of continuous return to flight remains consistent for all.
lessons.1.title: Understanding the T-38 Aircraft
lessons.1.summary: The twin-engine, two-seat supersonic trainer is a training device that allows for the repetition of speed, altitude, and abnormal attitudes in shorter cycles than a spacecraft.
lessons.1.body.0: NASA's Ellington Field aircraft description identifies the T-38 as a two-seat aircraft with two engines, a top speed of Mach 1.2, and a service ceiling of 50,000 feet. Originally an Air Force advanced trainer used as a step before moving to subsequent jets, NASA repurposed its characteristics for physical and cognitive acclimatization prior to spaceflight.
lessons.1.body.1: The aircraft is small, with limited visibility and operational margin. As speed increases, the time window for decision-making shrinks, requiring simultaneous monitoring of fuel, engines, and pressurization. This 'lack of margin' closely resembles the load experienced in orbit when procedures, timelines, and anomalies overlap.
lessons.1.body.2: Official photos show candidates lined up in front of an aircraft marked with the Artemis insignia on the tail. The trainer is not a display piece but an active flight proficiency device. Candidates begin with an external inspection, visually checking the condition of the landing gear, wings, air intakes, and canopy.
lessons.1.facts.0.label: Crew
lessons.1.facts.1.label: Top Speed
lessons.1.facts.2.label: Altitude
lessons.2.title: The two-seat aircraft is a classroom for Crew Resource Management
lessons.2.summary: The front and rear seats, ground control, and other aircraft in formation. Sharing voice, repeating back, and leaving no ambiguity in conversation share the same structure as the loops in a spacecraft.
lessons.2.body.0: Explanations from the Aircraft Operations Division state that the T-38 is a venue for learning crew coordination, internal and external communication, and the simultaneous processing of multiple operations. The division of labor, where the front seat pilots and the rear seat handles navigation and monitoring, mirrors the relationship between the Commander (CDR) and Flight Engineer (FE) reading procedures together in orbit.
lessons.2.body.1: Communications are short, pairing callsigns, intent, and responses. If a message is not heard clearly, do not proceed on assumption; repeat it back to confirm. In formation, one must read not only one's own position but also the energy and spacing of other aircraft. The conciseness required when astronauts speak with CAPCOM on the ground is embodied here.
lessons.2.body.2: For candidates without a pilot background, the first barrier is not the operation itself, but sharing 'who is looking at what, right now.' Official training includes both pilot training and the refinement of existing skills. Regardless of the path, cockpit communication discipline is evaluated by the same standards.
lessons.2.facts.0.label: Seats
lessons.2.facts.0.value: Front seat pilot / Rear seat monitor
lessons.2.facts.1.label: Skills
lessons.3.title: Preflight is the core of training that does not fly
lessons.3.summary: Inspections and briefings before taxiing are the last chance to spot anomalies on the ground. Candidates repeat the same habits even in the WB-57.
lessons.3.body.0: Official records for the 2025 class show candidates inspecting the WB-57 cockpit at Ellington Field, published as 'preflight checks.' They establish a sequence, manually trace the landing gear, hydraulics, fuel, pressurization, and ejection systems, and verbalize their findings. The time spent not flying determines flight safety.
lessons.3.body.1: Briefings cover weather, alternate airports, fuel plans, emergency rally points, and procedures for communication loss. Questions are resolved before takeoff. Just like the GO/NO-GO polls before a spacecraft launch, we do not accelerate with ambiguity.
lessons.3.body.2: Participating in maintenance is an extension of inspection. The 'Airspace' podcast explains that candidates handle aircraft in the maintenance area to prepare for the reality that external maintenance cannot be called for in orbit. The ability to report small leaks or loose parts found during inspection is part of flight fitness.
lessons.3.facts.0.label: Location
lessons.3.facts.1.label: Verification
lessons.4.title: Maintain spatial awareness under G-forces and abnormal attitudes
lessons.4.summary: Acceleration and rotation deceive the inner ear. Trusting instruments and crew voices rather than physical sensation to pitch the nose up is a rehearsal for orbital insertion and reentry.
lessons.4.body.0: Explanations from Ellington note that the aerobatic maneuvers of the T-38 have been used to acclimatize to the abnormal attitudes encountered in former Orbiter landings and spacecraft. Training materials also list adaptation to the G-environment of launch as a goal. In head-down acceleration, the sense of 'up' disappears, and without a visible horizon, the body lies.
lessons.4.body.1: The countermeasure is instrument cross-checking. Read attitude, speed, altitude, and thrust in a cycle, and call out to the other seat. In night vision or clouds, one must have the courage to ignore external views. In manual attitude control of spacecraft, there are moments when rate gyros are trusted before the view out the window.
lessons.4.body.2: Under high G, vision narrows, and the timing of anti-G maneuvers and breathing determines operational precision. Training looks not just at 'enduring' the forces, but at the ability to execute the next checklist item while enduring them.
lessons.4.facts.0.label: Goal
lessons.4.facts.1.label: Principle
lessons.4.facts.1.value: Prioritize instruments and readbacks over sensation
lessons.5.title: Learn low pressure and hypoxia first in the altitude chamber
lessons.5.summary: The chamber at the Sonny Carter Training Facility creates pressures from sea level to near-vacuum on the ground, allowing safe testing of high-altitude flight and space procedures.
lessons.5.body.0: The 2025 class entered Johnson's altitude chamber as part of flight training. Official articles describe the facility as capable of simulating pressures from sea-level atmospheric pressure to near-vacuum. Wearing flight suits and helmets, candidates acclimate to conditions faced in high-altitude flight and space, practicing procedures and interventions for safety.
lessons.5.body.1: At low pressure, gases in the body expand and partial pressure of oxygen drops. By memorizing on the ground one's initial symptoms—finger discomfort, slowed judgment, narrowed vision—and the sequence of mask switching, emergency descent, and reporting to the crew, one can avoid encountering symptoms for the first time during a high-altitude leg in the T-38. Monitors observe candidates from outside the chamber, and intervention is part of the training.
lessons.5.facts.0.label: Facility
lessons.5.facts.1.label: Range
lessons.5.deepDive.title: Why the chamber before flight
lessons.5.deepDive.body.0: At low pressure, gas expansion and hypoxia arrive simultaneously. By physically memorizing one's initial symptoms and the sequence of mask switching, emergency descent, and reporting to the crew on the ground, one can avoid encountering symptoms for the first time during a high-altitude leg in the T-38.
lessons.6.title: Land survival is insurance for remote landings
lessons.6.summary: To prepare for landing in sparsely populated areas after a mission, shelter, fire, water, and team roles are established in the field.
lessons.6.body.0: Candidates receive land and water survival training in case of an emergency landing in a remote area after a mission. The 2025 class conducted field training at Fort Rucker, Alabama, with official photos recording shelter construction. The 2013 class conducted a three-day field training near Rangeley, Maine, where fire-starting was introduced as a technique supporting survival.
lessons.6.body.1: The content of the training is not a camping hobby. Deciding who holds the map, who checks for injuries, and who signals is done first. Roles and rally points are fixed before fatigue and cold make conversation sloppy. As with emergency checklists for spacecraft, procedure comes before memory.
lessons.6.body.2: Johnson's introductory materials state that candidates walk through the wilderness, study geology in both classroom and field settings, and utilize simulations and virtual reality. Survival is not an isolated subject; it is a discipline that evaluates judgment and teamwork on the same scale as other training components.
lessons.6.facts.0.label: Recent Facilities
lessons.6.facts.1.label: Objective
lessons.6.facts.1.value: Survival and team cohesion after a remote landing
lessons.7.title: The First Minute After Water Landing Determines Survival
lessons.7.summary: After a capsule or aircraft enters the water, the primary challenge is to execute the sequence of egress, flotation, assembly, and hypothermia prevention without error.
lessons.7.body.0: Official 2011 explanations require the completion of military water survival training prior to the flight curriculum. Water adds weight to spacesuits and flight suits even under gravity, while simultaneously impairing vision and body temperature. The first priority is not swimming, but floating, breathing, counting crew members, and moving to the raft.
lessons.7.body.1: The 2025 class continued water survival training at Johnson's Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL). Official photos show candidates in orange flight suits and white helmets floating on small rafts, communicating with divers. The raft is not a destination; it is a workstation for signaling, observation, and treating injuries.
lessons.7.body.2: Post-water landing priorities are: airway, buoyancy, hypothermia, assembly, and being found. Currents and wind will drift the raft. Since anchoring is often impossible, plans for drift direction, sunlight exposure, and water supply must be established quickly. In spacecraft water recovery operations, this same principle of 'survive first, then be found' serves as the point of contact with recovery teams.
lessons.7.facts.0.label: Sequence
lessons.7.facts.0.value: Water training before the flight curriculum
lessons.7.facts.1.label: Location
lessons.8.title: NBL Storms and Hoisting Are Rehearsals for Recovery
lessons.8.summary: Simulated storms and helicopter hoisting in large pools practice the entire process, including the 'handover' action after being found.
lessons.8.body.0: Official articles explicitly state that part of the water training is conducted in simulated storms within the NBL. In conditions of waves, wind, and noise, roles defined in briefings can break down. Positions for gripping the raft edge, responsibilities for bailing water, and assignments for signal mirrors or radios must be reconfirmed under the assumption that voices cannot be heard.
lessons.8.body.1: Other official photos show candidates wearing flotation devices being hoisted out of the pool and seated in rescue baskets. Being found is not the end point. Signals for the hoist, arm positioning, and postures to avoid entanglement in rotating cables are repeated under the instructions of divers and ground crews.
lessons.8.body.2: The NBL is primarily a facility for neutral buoyancy training for spacewalks. Using the same tank for water landing training holds significance beyond mere facility convenience. A shared culture of safety divers, time limits, and abort criteria applies to both EVA and water landing operations.
lessons.8.facts.0.label: Environment
lessons.8.facts.1.label: Skills
lessons.9.title: The Judgment Patterns Cultivated by Flight and Survival
lessons.9.summary: Whether in the T-38, the wilderness, or the water, the goal is not heroism, but creating reflexes that return to procedures when information is lacking.
lessons.9.body.0: The 2025 class, halfway through a roughly two-year curriculum, is simultaneously progressing through geology, flight, chamber, and water training, while also studying Russian, cross-cultural training, spacecraft systems, extravehicular activity, emergency procedures, and maintenance/repair. Official announcements state that upon graduation, candidates will possess the foundation of operational expertise, science, and technology, whether for the ISS or the Moon.
lessons.9.body.1: Flight aptitude training is not a competition of 'flying fast.' It involves not skipping inspections, returning to instruments in abnormal attitudes, and re-declaring roles in the water. All of these contribute to the ability to convey a situation to CAPCOM in a single sentence when alarms overlap in orbit.
lessons.9.body.2: Before advancing to the next subject, record your own weaknesses. These include spatial awareness, communication under hypothermia, and verbalizing maintenance observations. The candidate curriculum is also an evaluation period. Official explanations note that final astronaut certification depends on the successful completion of this period.
lessons.9.facts.0.label: 2025 Class Graduation
lessons.9.facts.1.label: Evaluation
lessons.9.facts.1.value: Completion of training and evaluation is a prerequisite
quiz.0.prompt: According to NASA's Ellington Field explanation, what is the top speed of the T-38?
quiz.0.explanation: The official fact sheet states that the T-38 reaches Mach 1.2 and can climb to an altitude of 50,000 feet.
quiz.1.prompt: According to the official explanation by Aircraft Operations, when did NASA begin using the T-38 for astronaut training?
quiz.1.explanation: The official podcast 'Airspace' states that NASA adopted the T-38 in the early 1960s and has continued to use it since.
quiz.2.prompt: According to a 2011 official NASA explanation, what is the approximate monthly flight time guideline for pilot astronauts in the T-38?
quiz.2.explanation: The 'Astronaut Selection and Training' explanation notes that pilots fly 15 hours per month, while non-pilots fly a minimum of 4 hours per month.
quiz.3.prompt: In the same official explanation, what is the minimum monthly T-38 flight time required for non-pilot astronauts?
quiz.3.explanation: Non-pilots fly a minimum of 4 hours per month. The policy indicates that all astronauts are expected to return to the flight environment continuously.
quiz.4.prompt: Which airfield is officially cited as the center of flight operations at Johnson Space Center?
quiz.4.explanation: The Ellington Field aircraft description states that this airfield is the center of JSC flight operations, with astronaut training as its primary function.
quiz.5.prompt: What physical load does the official training explanation state is simulated by the T-38?
quiz.5.choices.0: Bone mass loss due to long-term weightlessness
quiz.5.choices.1: G-forces similar to those during launch
quiz.5.choices.3: High-pressure oxygen in the deep sea
quiz.5.explanation: The training explanation notes that the T-38 is used for acclimatization to the flight environment and adaptation to the G-forces experienced during launch.
quiz.6.prompt: What training does the 2011 official explanation require to be completed before starting the flight curriculum?
quiz.6.explanation: Candidates complete military water survival before the flight syllabus and also obtain scuba certification in preparation for EVAs.
quiz.7.prompt: For the 2025 class's water survival training, which facility does the official article cite as the location?
quiz.7.choices.0: A live ship in the Atlantic Ocean
quiz.7.explanation: The official article on summer training documents raft operations, simulated storms, and hoisting from the water at NBL.
quiz.8.prompt: Which location is officially recorded as the site for the 2025 class's land survival training?
quiz.8.choices.2: Rio Grande del Norte (geology training site)
quiz.8.explanation: Official Johnson articles and class introductions show field survival and shelter construction at Fort Rucker, Alabama. Maine is a record from the 2013 class.
quiz.9.prompt: What pressure range does the official article state can be simulated in the altitude chamber?
quiz.9.choices.0: From sea level to aircraft cruising altitude only
quiz.9.choices.1: From sea level to near vacuum
quiz.9.choices.2: Fixed at ISS cabin pressure (1 atm)
quiz.9.explanation: Johnson's chamber simulates pressures from sea level to near vacuum, allowing practice of high-altitude flight and space procedures.
quiz.10.prompt: Which facility is officially noted as the location where the 2025 class conducted altitude chamber training?
quiz.10.explanation: Official photo captions identify the altitude chamber at the Sonny Carter Training Facility in Houston.
quiz.11.prompt: What element does the official description of Aircraft Operations emphasize as being learned in the T-38?
quiz.11.explanation: The T-38 is officially described as a place to learn crew coordination, internal and external communication, and handling multiple operations.
quiz.12.prompt: What is the T-38's service ceiling indicated in the Ellington Field description?
quiz.12.explanation: The official fact sheet states an altitude of 50,000 feet. High altitude requires simultaneous management of pressurization and low oxygen.
quiz.13.prompt: Regarding the Artemis II crew's T-38 training, what effect does the official article emphasize?
quiz.13.choices.1: Spatial awareness and adaptability under high-load, dynamic flight conditions
quiz.13.choices.3: Nutrition management in long-term closed environments
quiz.13.explanation: The 'Preparing for Artemis II' article states that the T-38 develops spatial awareness and adaptability to high-load, dynamic flight conditions, directly connecting to judgment under pressure in space.
quiz.14.prompt: What is the priority action taught in this lesson immediately after water landing?
quiz.14.choices.0: Swim to shore at full speed
quiz.14.choices.1: First take photos to record location
quiz.14.choices.2: Float, breathe, count heads, and move to the raft
quiz.14.explanation: Water adds weight to clothing and causes heat loss. The initial priority is not covering distance, but maintaining buoyancy, breathing, and assembling the group. Official training also emphasizes raft use and team decision-making.
quiz.15.prompt: According to the official summer report, when is the 2025 astronaut candidate class expected to graduate?
quiz.15.explanation: Official articles state that the class is on track to graduate in 2027, after which they will join the active astronaut corps.
glossary.0.description: Training using aircraft such as the T-38 to develop spatial awareness, G-tolerance, and crew coordination through high-load flight, aligning the body and habits with the operational demands of spaceflight.
glossary.1.description: A twin-engine, two-seat supersonic trainer. NASA has used it for astronaut flight proficiency since the early 1960s.
glossary.2.description: The flight operations hub for the Johnson Space Center. Training and research aircraft such as the T-38 and WB-57 are based here.
glossary.3.description: A framework for communication and decision-making that uses role division, read-backs, raising concerns, and workload distribution to achieve safety levels exceeding individual skill.
glossary.4.description: A series of checks and briefings before takeoff to verify aircraft condition, weather, fuel, alternate airports, and communication loss procedures.
glossary.5.description: A facility that simulates pressure from sea level to near-vacuum on the ground, allowing safe experience of symptoms and countermeasures for hypoxia and low pressure.
glossary.6.description: Originally a water tank for EVA training. Recent official records indicate it is also used for water survival rafts and simulated storms.
glossary.7.description: Training to prepare for remote landings by establishing shelter, fire, water, and role division in the field. Recently conducted at locations such as Fort Rucker.
glossary.8.description: A long-range, high-altitude research aircraft used for research flights since the 1960s. It was also used in the flight training of the 2025 class.
glossary.9.description: After selection, individuals undergo approximately two years of basic training in flight, EVA, systems, medicine, geology, and languages, and become astronauts after passing evaluations.
